extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, advanced students, and readers of 19th-century mathematical journals interested in analytic geometry, conic sections, spherical projections, and symmetric functions
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of theorems, propositions, and methodological remarks in analytic and synthetic geometry, spherical projections, properties of conics, symmetric functions, and spiral curves, together with techniques for algebraic transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of projected circles on Mercator's chart
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three forms assumed by the projected circles of the sphere according as they include, do not include, or pass through one of the poles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) If the circle does not include a pole: projected form similar to projection of a great circle — a waving form, symmetrically placed above and below a certain parallel of latitude (the latitude of which can be determined). 2) If the circle includes one pole: projected form is an elliptical form, arcs represented equal above and below the right line representing the parallel. 3) If the circle passes through the pole: projected curve has two infinite branches, vertex on the parallel of least latitude, with meridians 90° distant from the meridian of the vertex as asymptotes. Equations and integrals for each case are given; limiting behavior as highest latitude increases matches great-circle case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and analytic properties of circles that include a pole
rubrics_metrics.description: When a circle to be projected includes one of the poles, its projection reduces to expressions of same form as the great circle case (after substitution cosec^2 a for sin^2 x), yielding y = + log cot{45° − 1/2 a} (with sign determined by longitudes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use derived integrals and substitutions (e.g., tan a · cos z substitutions) to obtain explicit projected-form equations; note parity and sign changes for longitudes differing by 180°.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic description of 'second form' projected curves (elliptical form)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the second form (elliptical projected circles), dy/dx relations reduce to sin z = k sin φ (constant k), and the length of these curves is expressed by an elliptic function of the first order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set k = sin X (a constant less than 1) and make necessary substitutions to express ds and integrals in elliptic-function form. Radius of curvature and evolute coordinates admit simple expressions; radius varies from sin X to tan X (sine to tangent of maximum longitude).

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for two equal tangents to a parabola
rubrics_metrics.description: Two equal tangents drawn from a point (a, b) to the parabola y^2 = 4 m x can only be drawn (non-degenerately) when the point lies in the principal axis produced (i.e., b = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic elimination of chord-of-contact and perpendicular leads to condition B'(B^2 − 4 a m) = 0; the factor b = 0 is the required condition for two distinct equal tangents from an exterior point. The other factor b^2 = 4 a m corresponds to the point lying on the parabola itself (degenerate case where tangents coalesce).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: equal tangents to ellipse and hyperbola
rubrics_metrics.description: For an ellipse (or hyperbola) two equal tangents can only be drawn from a point without the curve when that point lies on the major or minor axis produced; special case a = b (circle): two equal tangents can be drawn from any external point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply analogous algebraic reductions (as for the parabola) to the general second-order curve; identify axis conditions (a = 0 or b = 0 in coordinate parametrizations) as loci permitting equal tangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological Scholium: retain all algebraic factors during reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: In analytical or coordinate investigations one must retain and subsequently examine every factor that may enter into an investigation; suppressing factors in preliminary reductions may remove the means of determining important cases of the locus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not discard multiplicative factors (e.g., a or b^2) early; keep them through reductions so that special, degenerate, or boundary cases can be identified and analyzed afterwards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition (Investigation of Exercise 150) — fixed-point from chords through fixed points
rubrics_metrics.description: Let AB, BC be chords in a conic passing through fixed points P and Q respectively; draw AD parallel to PQ and join DC cutting PQ in R; then R is a fixed point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via choosing a fixed auxiliary line QE cutting the curve in E,F and comparing semidiameters or chord ratios in ellipse/hyperbola/parabola; leads to QR·QP : QE·QF :: OG^2 : OK^2 so QR·QP is a given rectangle and R is fixed. Use corresponding semidiameter or chord constructions depending on conic type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition — quadrilateral with three sides through fixed collinear points
rubrics_metrics.description: If three sides of a quadrilateral inscribed in a conic always pass through three points P,Q,S situated in a straight line, then the fourth side will also pass through a fixed point situated in the same straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw AD parallel to PQ and join DC meeting PQ in R (by previous prop. R is fixed); then use intersections and parallels to deduce the fixed point on the fourth side. This is a geometric (Desargues-related) involution-type property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition — polygon inscribed in circle with many sides through fixed collinear points
rubrics_metrics.description: If a hexagon is inscribed in a circle and five of its sides pass through five fixed points in the same straight line, then the sixth side will always pass through a fixed point in the same straight line; the result generalizes to 2n-gons (even-sided polygons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces hexagon to two quadrilaterals by drawing a diagonal; apply quadrilateral property successively to show diagonals and remaining sides pass through fixed points. Concludes that the problem is either indeterminate or impossible depending on the specific positions (porismatic behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to Desargues' theorem and involution (when line cuts or touches conic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorem about polygons with sides through fixed collinear points may be deduced from Desargues' general theorem on involution, provided the line in which the points are situated either cuts or touches the conic; when the line neither cuts nor touches the conic a modification or auxiliary points are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two modes: (a) extend Desargues’ theorem to intersections of the line with polygon sides independently of intersections with the conic, or (b) find two points in the line representing intersections with a subsidiary conic that merge appropriately when tangency occurs. Consult Matthew Stewart's demonstration (Simson’s Conic Sections) for case constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of critical symmetric functions for transformations of equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical functions (of degrees 1,2,3,4, etc.) can be formed so that certain combinations cause coefficients of a transformed equation to be free from a chosen parameter P; these critical functions are used to produce transformations of a general equation into another with desired coefficient constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct combinations (for example, form 6 + λ B' (n−3) p_r to remove higher powers of P), choose multipliers (λ) to force coefficients (like E) to vanish independently of relations among the quantities, and thereby obtain critical functions (explicit polynomials are given for degrees up to four). Use these critical equations first (often a quadratic) to determine Q, then obtain P from a linear equation — this yields transformations solvable by simple equations rather than full elimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical procedure for transforming a 2t-degree equation via y = P + Q a^r + ...
rubrics_metrics.description: To transform the general equation of degree 2t in x to one in y connected by y = P + Q a^r + R a^{2r}+..., impose coefficient conditions (e.g., eliminate dependence on P) and determine Q from a simple quadratic (the critical equation) then determine P from the remaining linear equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the transformed coefficients in terms of critical functions C1, C2, C3; substituting these yields solvable systems (quadratic and linear, or cubic/biquadratic if replacing by higher critical functions). The critical equation must be solved first; no other elimination is necessary for the presented classes of transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and relations among several named critical symmetric functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit forms are given for critical symmetric functions of second, third and fourth degree (named C1, C2, C3 or symbols A, B, B') and relations among them (linear combinations and normalization divisions) that preserve criticality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may divide functions by powers (e.g., divide A by 2^n, p' by 3^n, B by 24^n) to get alternative normalized critical functions better adapted for transformations; explicit coefficient relations and recurrence-type relations are provided in the text for practical computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and properties of proposed new spirals (hyperbolic, Archimedean, elliptic, circular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various spiral families are defined and related: reciprocal/hyperbolic spiral (rθ = a b), Archimedean (r = a θ) as rectilinear spiral, elliptic spiral (a r + b θ = a' b' form) and circular spiral (degenerate case). Relations: hyperbolic spiral asymptotic to Archimedean; elliptic spiral finite and contained in circle of radius a; formulae for tangent, subtangent, normal, subnormal and area given for special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parameter substitutions (change of exponent parameters) to move between families; compute tangents, subtangents, normals, subnormals and area via derived formulae in each special case; note degeneration/special cases when parameters take particular values (e.g., a=b yields circular spiral).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern geometry propositions about lines parallel to a plane (XLV–XLIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of propositions: (XLV) If three straight lines are parallel to one plane and no two are in one plane, then all straight lines resting upon them will be divided proportionally. (XLVI) Under same hypothesis, all straight lines resting upon them will be parallel to another plane. (XLVII) The same hypotheses yield proportional divisions for other triplets. (XLVIII) For a twisted quadrilateral with opposite sides divided in the same ratios, lines PQ and MN lie in same plane and intersect at S with PS:SQ = BM:MC and MS:SN = BP:PA. (XLIX) A line moving parallel to a plane and always resting upon two lines which meet that plane generates the hyperbolic paraboloid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof techniques employ constructing auxiliary parallel planes and transversals, using proportionality of segments, similarity of triangles, and parallelogram relations. For the hyperbolic paraboloid generation, take two fixed lines meeting the plane and let a line move parallel to the plane while always touching the two fixed lines; locus is a ruled (hyperbolic) paraboloid.
